### Egypt in the lead while Nigeria regains territory. South Africa - and to a lesser extent Kenya - underperform.
[Max Cuvellier Giacomelli](https://substack.com/@maxatbd)

Jul 20, 2026

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!hoS5!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6dcb9abe-e06f-4e18-bd16-e9a3830d565c_3000x3062.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!hoS5!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6dcb9abe-e06f-4e18-bd16-e9a3830d565c_3000x3062.png)

# October: Morocco and Tanzania make a splash
### 34 start-ups raised $183m in October, and for once, more than half of it went to ventures based outside the Big Four
[![Max Cuvellier Giacomelli's avatar](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!leFZ!,w_36,h_36,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F25aa0c11-0da6-4bfc-b8e1-5e5e390031e5_670x670.png)](https://substack.com/@maxatbd)

[Max Cuvellier Giacomelli](https://substack.com/@maxatbd)

Nov 05, 2026

9

4

3

Share

In October, 34 start-ups in Africa announced funding of $100k or more, for a combined $183m (exc. exits). It is -24% compared with September ($241m) and -29% below the average of the previous 12 months ($259m/month). It is also well behind October 2025 ($435m, -58% YoY), when Spiro and Moniepoint had raised $100m and $90m respectively. Deal activity was also below par: 34 ventures, vs. an average of 43 per month over the past year.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!dI8D!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fcab0985e-f507-4e38-b82f-06f7c2992b27_2172x1688.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!dI8D!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fcab0985e-f507-4e38-b82f-06f7c2992b27_2172x1688.png)

Equity represented $110m (60%) of the money raised, debt $71m (39%) and grants around $2m. They were followed by a string of debt deals: a $17m [bond issuance by ValU](https://efgholding.com/en/media/news/Valu23rdbond) in Egypt, $13m for [Afreenergy Solar](https://africanenergycouncil.org/afreenergy-solar-secures-e12-million-to-expand-solar-power-in-senegal/) in Senegal, an $11m loan from Finnfund to [Bisedge](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/bisedge-secures-10-million-long-term-loan-from-finnfund-to-expand-electric-intralogistics-fleet-in-nigeria-and-east-africa-302902397.html) and a $10m EBRD loan to [Beacon Power Services](https://www.startupresearcher.com/news/ebrd-backs-beacon-power-services-with-usd10-million-smart-metering-loan) (both in Nigeria). Climate tech start-ups claimed 55% of the funding.

Geographically, October was unusual. Start-ups based in the Big Four raised “only” 46% of the funding, their lowest monthly share since November 2022. The Big Four still accounted for 26 of the 34 start-ups raising $100k+ though. In value, Nigeria came first ($42m across 9 start-ups, mostly energy and mobility debt), but Morocco and Tanzania were right behind ($40m each), followed by Egypt ($19m) and Senegal ($13m). _One month doesn’t make a trend… but it’s a nice teaser for an upcoming post on who could be the “Next” markets we will be publishing shortly…_

There were also four exits in October: [MNT-Halan’s IPO](https://enterpriseam.com/egypt/2026/10/07/mnts-subscriptions-open-today-at-egp-24-5-per-share/) on the Egyptian Exchange ($1.4b market cap at the time of writing), HealthPay’s [acquisition of PeacePay](https://egyptinnovate.com/en/news/healthpay-purchases-peacepay-technology-and-solutions-to-advance-e-commerce-payments-in-egypt) (Egypt), GiG Software completing its [acquisition of 888Africa](https://www.gig.com/ir-news/completion-of-888africa-acquisition/) (Mozambique), and the [sale of LekkeSlaap](https://www.moneyweb.co.za/news/companies-and-deals/lekkeslaap-sold-to-sa-investors-as-co-founders-exit/) to South African investors (South Africa). The [surprise last-minute halting of OPay’s NY listing](https://launchbaseafrica.com/2026/11/05/chinese-rules-opay-and-a-halted-new-york-listing/) is a developing story. The 2026 tally is now at 38 exits, vs. 42 over the same period last year.

Zooming out, start-ups in Africa have now raised $2.4b in Jan–Oct 2026, -12% compared with the same period in 2025 ($2.7b). The gap has widened since the end of September, mostly because October 2025 was such a strong month. Equity is still up (+5% YoY, at $1.6b), while debt is down -33% ($740m vs. $1.1b). The breadth indicators remain weak comparatively: 343 start-ups have raised $100k+ so far this year, vs. 438 in Jan–Oct 2025 (-22% YoY). It is the lowest Jan–Oct tally since we started tracking $100k+ deals in 2021. The number of named active investors is down too, from 442+ to 370+ (-16% YoY).

With two months to go, matching 2025’s total ($3.2b) would require $814m in funding to be announced in November and December, vs. $496m over the same two months last year. In other words, this is quite unlikely. However, on the equity side, $338m is all it would take to beat 2025 ($1.9b), which is less than two months at the average pace of the past year. 2026 could therefore end up as the best year for equity since 2022…

_If you’d like to dig deeper into the October 2026 deals (and the 4,700+ others we have been tracking since 2019) by country, sector, stage or instrument, they’re all in our [deals database](https://thebigdeal.gumroad.com/l/bQSRD/africabigdeal), updated monthly (with a 10% discount for you readers)._ _I’ll leave you with a short poll below to get the temperature in the room._ _Bonne journée!_ _[Ma](https://www.linkedin.com/in/mcuvellier/)_ [x](https://www.linkedin.com/in/mcuvellier/)

POLL

### How will 2026 close?

# Nigeria Tops Africa Startup Funding at $635M [2026]
![Laura Bennett](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/lbennett.webp)

[Laura Bennett](https://shattered.io/author/lbennett/)

Updated Oct 23, 2026 · 17 min read

[Share on X](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2Fnigeria-tops-africa-startup-funding-635-million-2026%2F&text=Nigeria%20Tops%20Africa%20Startup%20Funding%20at%20%24635M%20%5B2026%5D)[Share on Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2Fnigeria-tops-africa-startup-funding-635-million-2026%2F)[Share on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2Fnigeria-tops-africa-startup-funding-635-million-2026%2F)[Share on Reddit](https://www.reddit.com/submit?url=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2Fnigeria-tops-africa-startup-funding-635-million-2026%2F&title=Nigeria%20Tops%20Africa%20Startup%20Funding%20at%20%24635M%20%5B2026%5D)[Copy link](https://shattered.io/nigeria-tops-africa-startup-funding-635-million-2026/)

![Nigeria Tops Africa Startup Funding at $635M](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/nigeria-tops-africa-startup-funding-635-million-2026-gen-1024x585.webp)

Nigerian startups raised **$635 million** between January and September 2026, according to data from the tracker Africa: The Big Deal, and that total puts Nigeria back at the top of the continent’s startup-funding table. [BusinessDay reported](https://businessday.ng/technology/article/nigeria-reclaims-africas-startup-funding-lead-as-investment-hits-635m/) that the result is Nigeria’s first lead in African startup funding since 2022. Reports published on October 21 put the figure at 2.6 times the $247 million Nigerian startups raised in the same nine months of 2025.

The deal count rose too, though far less sharply. A total of 77 Nigerian ventures raised funding in the period, up from 70 a year earlier. That gap between a 157% jump in dollars and a 10% rise in deals tells most of the story, because a handful of very large rounds carried the headline number.

This analysis breaks down what the data does and does not show, who took the money, how Egypt’s $445 million compares, and why developers, tooling vendors and engineering leaders should care. Capital is flowing to emerging-market founders well beyond Lagos, as a recent [$300K pre-seed for a Saudi event-tech startup](https://shattered.io/inve-saudi-event-tech-300k-pre-seed-outliers-vc-2026/) showed. Still, Nigeria startup funding is now the clearest signal of where African software demand is heading.

![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)·

## Nigeria Startup Funding Versus 2025: 2.6 Times the Money
The year-over-year comparison is the cleanest part of the data. Nigerian startups raised $247 million in January through September 2025 and $635 million in the same window of 2026. That is an increase of $388 million, or about 157%. [Nairametrics framed the result](https://nairametrics.com/2026/10/21/nigeria-reclaims-africas-startup-funding-lead-as-investments-rise-to-635-million/) as a rise in investment to $635 million, and several other Nigerian outlets used near-identical language on October 21.

The table below puts the two periods side by side. The average-per-venture row is simple division of the reported totals by the reported deal counts, so treat it as a rough indicator and not as a median. Averages in venture data run high when a few large rounds sit at the top.

## Egypt Closes In: $445 Million in Second Place
| Group (Jan-Sep 2026) | Amount raised | Share of Africa total (derived) |
|-|-|-|
| All African startups | about $2.16 billion | 100% |
| Nigeria | $635 million | about 29.4% |
| Egypt | $445 million | about 20.6% |
| Nigeria and Egypt combined | $1.08 billion | 50.0% |
| Moove, Flutterwave, Jumia, Yellow Card combined | $440 million | about 20.4% |
| Rest of Nigeria (73 ventures) | about $195 million | about 9.0% |
| All other markets and pan-African ventures | about $1.08 billion | 50.0% |

## What to Watch Next
Three items will clarify the picture in coming weeks. First, individual company disclosures. If Moove, Flutterwave, Jumia or Yellow Card publish round sizes, investors and journalists can replace the group total with named figures. Second, a split between equity and debt, which would show how much of the $635 million funds engineering growth versus lending capacity.

Third, the fourth-quarter pipeline. Egypt needs large rounds to overtake, and Nigeria needs its mid-size companies to close more deals to avoid relying on four names. Tracking announcements against the Africa: The Big Deal threshold will show whether the lead widens or erodes.

For readers who build software, the working conclusion is practical. Nigeria’s startup funding is bigger and more concentrated than it was a year ago. Funded companies buy tools, hire engineers and demand reliable infrastructure. The vendors and teams that understand that shift will find buyers. Those who read only the headline will miss how uneven the funding underneath really is.

## FAQ: Nigeria Startup Funding in 2026
### How much did Nigerian startups raise in the first nine months of 2026?
Nigerian startups raised $635 million between January and September 2026, according to Africa: The Big Deal data cited by Nigerian and African outlets. Reports published on October 21 gave the figure.

### How does that compare with 2025?
The 2026 total is 2.6 times the $247 million raised in the same period of 2025. The number of ventures raising at least $100,000 rose from 70 to 77.

### How much did all of Africa raise?
African startups collectively raised approximately $2.16 billion between January and September 2026. Nigeria and Egypt together account for $1.08 billion, or half of that total.

### What does Africa: The Big Deal track?
The tracker monitors African startups that raise at least $100,000. Smaller rounds fall below its threshold and do not count toward the totals quoted in this article.

# And then? 🔭 Looking for Africa’s “Next” markets
### 35% of the start-ups raising $100k+ in Africa are now based outside the Big Four, but they attract only 15% of the funding. Which markets are getting to critical mass?
Nov 16, 2026

In Q1-Q3 2026, 35% of the start-ups raising $100k+ were based outside the Big Four, up from 24% five years ago.

33 Moroccan start-ups have raised a round of $1m or more over the period, more than in any other market outside the Big Four, and 6 have raised a $10m+ round, the latest being ABA Life’s $40m raise in October.

Funded by the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) and implemented by GIZ and DEG Impulse, the programme provides start-ups with up to €100k in non-dilutive funding (i.e. grants), provided they raise at least the same amount from private investors, and up to €200k in performance-based top-ups.

But with few local investors and one exit each, they scored lower than their peers, even if Tanzania’s funding is up +30% since 2025, thanks to East Africa Foods’ $40m Series B in October (Rwanda’s is down -65%).

### We're in 2036, one market has grown so much we're now talking about the Big Five. Which one is it?
Senegal

![](https://techeconomy.ng/media-proxy/uploads/African%20startup%20funding%20October%202026-900x600.png)Source: Magnific

African startups raised $183 million in October 2026, with ventures outside the continent’s traditional investment hubs attracting more than half of the disclosed funding.

Data from Africa: The Big Deal shows that 34 startups secured at least $100,000 during the month, raising 24% less than September’s $241 million altogether.

The recent numbers for October also fell 29% below the previous 12-month monthly average of $259 million.

However, based on the geographical distribution of the funding, Egypt, Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa, collectively known as the Big Four, attracted just 46% of October’s total.

This is their lowest combined share since November 2022 and also differs sharply from 2025, when the four markets accounted for 82% of Africa’s total startup funding.

East Africa Foods attracted investment from InfraCo Africa, Oikocredit and FMO, among other investors. Together, the two companies accounted for $80 million, representing almost 44% of October’s funding.

Nigeria still recorded the highest country total, with $42 million raised across nine startups. A large part of the money went to energy and mobility businesses through debt financing.

The funding also showed how much African startups relied on different financing options during the month. Equity investments accounted for $110 million, or 60% of the total. Debt contributed $71 million, representing 39%, while grants accounted for approximately $2 million.

Senegal's Afreenergy Solar secured $13 million, while Bisedge obtained an $11 million loan from Finnfund.

In Nigeria, Beacon Power Services received a $10 million loan from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD).

[Climate technology](https://techeconomy.ng/africa-climatetech-funding-hits-6-35bn-as-sector-overtakes-fintech-in-venture-investment) companies also attracted a significant share of the money. The sector accounted for 55% of October's total funding, sustaining its strong showing across the African startup market.

The sector also overtook fintech as the continent's largest funding category that year.

## African startup funding still below 2025 levels
Despite October's geographical spread, the funding figures reveal that African startups are still finding it difficult to match last year's performance.

Between January and October 2026, startups raised $2.4 billion, compared with $2.7 billion during the same period in 2025. This represents a 12% decline.

On the difference between equity and debt financing, Equity funding increased by 5% year-on-year to $1.6 billion. Debt financing, however, dropped by 33%, falling from $1.1 billion to $740 million.

This follows a strong year for debt financing in 2025. Africa: The Big Deal reported that debt accounted for 37% of total startup funding that year, its highest proportion on record.

Partech's 2025 Africa Tech Venture Capital Report also put debt financing at a record $1.6 billion, representing 41% of capital deployed.

The number of funded businesses has also declined. Only 343 startups raised at least $100,000 between January and October 2026. During the same period last year, 438 businesses reached that threshold, representing a 22% drop.

The number of active investors also fell, as Africa: The Big Deal identified more than 370 active investors this year, compared with over 442 in the corresponding period of 2025.

The current figures come after African startup funding recovered in 2025. The continent raised $3.2 billion that year, recording a 40% increase after two years of contraction.

However, matching that annual total in 2026 will require a much stronger finish. Startups must announce another $814 million in November and December to equal last year's figure.

For comparison, African startups raised $496 million across those two months in 2025.

Equity financing has a more achievable target. Another $338 million would take 2026 equity funding above the $1.9 billion recorded in 2025. This is still possible at the average monthly pace of the past year.

## Four startup exits recorded in October
October also recorded four notable exits across Africa's technology sector.

Its market capitalisation stood at $1.4 billion at the time of reporting.

HealthPay also acquired PeacePay in Egypt, while GiG Software completed its acquisition of Mozambique-based 888Africa.

In South Africa, local investors acquired accommodation platform LekkeSlaap as its co-founders exited the business.

These transactions bring Africa's recorded startup exits to 38 in 2026. The continent recorded 42 exits during the corresponding period in 2025.

Meanwhile, reports that OPay's planned New York listing has been halted have added another development to the African fintech market. The circumstances surrounding the reported halt are a developing story.

Although October delivered a smaller funding total than previous months, Morocco and Tanzania's performance offers a different picture of where investment is going.

web.title: Nigerian Startups Reclaim Top Spot in Africa With $635M
web.description:
# Nigerian Startups Reclaim Top Spot in Africa as Funding Hits $635 Million in 2026
![Omorogie Alele](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/8d049b3679fac95bea9a0f07c444d6414c6232c70324d5860615e35149a06143?s=96&d=mm&r=g)

By [Omorogie Alele](https://ventureburn.com/author/adele/)

22 October 2026

[![google-news](https://ventureburn.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/google-news-icon.png)](https://news.google.com/publications/CAAqKggKIiRDQklTRlFnTWFoRUtEM1psYm5SMWNtVmlkWEp1TG1OdmJTZ0FQAQ?ceid=US:en&oc=3)

Key Takeaways

- Nigeria secured $635M in startup funding so far in 2026 to reclaim the number one position.
- The total funding was led by 4 massive scale-ups contributing 69% of the total startup funding.
- Rival tech hubs like Kenya and South Africa faced catastrophic funding declines since 2025.

## The Heavyweights Driving the Mega-Rounds
Africa: The Big Deal [reported](https://thebigdeal.substack.com/p/q32026c) that Nigerian startups pulled in $635 million through the first three months, taking the top spot. This sudden explosion of cash is far from a spray-and-pray operation.

Investors are definitely writing massive checks, but they are aiming them exclusively at proven scale-ups with serious traction. Four specific companies accounted for 69% of the national total: up $440 million.

[Moove](https://ventureburn.com/moove-250-million-to-lead-robotaxi-industry/), the mobility financing giant, led the charge with a jaw-dropping $250 million haul. Fintech behemoth [Flutterwave](https://ventureburn.com/flutterwave-raises-250m-series-e/) followed closely, locking down $100 million despite ongoing market adjustments.

Rounding out the top tier, e-commerce veteran Jumia bagged $50 million, while crypto infrastructure platform [Yellow Card](https://ventureburn.com/2022/08/yellow-card-simplifies-money-transfers-through-crypto-rails/) secured $40 million. You really have to look at the underlying message here. It proves that late-stage growth capital is still very much alive in Africa.

**_More Updates:_** [**_Legora Raises $550 Million To Challenge Rival Harvey_**](https://ventureburn.com/legora-raises-550-million-to-rival-harvey-ai/)

web.title: Grants for Female Entrepreneurs in Africa: Data and Statistics
web.description:
When our research team began tracking funding for women-led businesses across the continent, one fact kept standing out.

Outline

Venture capital tells the same story. Africa: The Big Deal found that in 2025, [startups founded only by women, or by all-female teams, received less than 1% of total funding, while all-male teams captured 91%](https://www.tekedia.com/african-startup-funding-in-2025-gender-gap-deepens-as-women-led-startups-attract-less-funding/). The data points the other way.

This is where grants come in, and it is important.

## Why Women Entrepreneurs in Africa Still Struggle to Get Funding
4. **Startup funding.** Africa: The Big Deal has tracked 2,808 equity deals since 2019. [About 25% involved a startup with at least one female co-founder, but those startups received only 17% of the funding](https://guardian.ng/business-services/female-startups-get-only-17-per-cent-deals-in-six-years/). The gap widens in bigger rounds, because female-led startups find it harder to raise large amounts as they grow. In 2025, [only 2.2% of total funding went to startups led by a woman CEO](https://guardian.ng/?p=2781423), the lowest share since tracking began in 2019.
